cases.title: Alif Partners
cases.subtitle: Products, requests and delivery in the partner workspace

meta.Команда: Product Designer, UX Researcher, Product Owner

context.title: The partner network was growing
context.text: Alif runs instalment plans through partner stores and the Alif Shop marketplace. Stores handled orders through an admin panel, terminals and bank employees. As the number of orders grew, so did the load on the call centre and the moderators.

task.title: More independence for the store
task.text: I designed a workspace where a partner can handle products, requests and delivery. Bank employees had to keep their tools for checking data and helping partners.

sections.title: How we made sense of the partner’s work

paragraphs: Before moving into design I worked in Alif’s call centre and partner department. That experience helped me work through the stores’ everyday tasks together with a UX researcher.

steps.title: We drew on first-hand experience
steps.text: I knew the process from the call centre and the partner department.

steps.title: We talked to the people involved
steps.text: 8 moderators, 7 leading partners and 2 CDO managers.

steps.title: We singled out two tasks
steps.text: Prepare the store’s offer and handle an incoming order.

blocks.subhead: What we heard in the interviews
paragraphs: The table collects the answers about requests, the catalogue and delivery. Two directions came out of those answers, and both are shown below.

figures.caption: Partners’ answers about working with the catalogue, requests and delivery. Research material from the project.

points.title: Adding a product
points.text: A partner looked the product up on Alif Shop and copied the SKU into the admin panel. In the new scenario the search moved inside the add-product step.

points.title: Handing over an order
points.text: It was unclear where to find a processed request and what to do about self-pickup. Delivery and self-pickup got separate paths.

sections.title: Sections built around the store’s tasks

paragraphs: Navigation was built around stores, products, requests, delivery and reviews. Moderators kept a separate data-checking section.

figures.caption: Sections of the partner and moderator workspace.

paragraphs: Search became the first step of adding a product. If the product is already in the catalogue, the partner finds it inside the workspace and sets their own offer: price, stock and terms. Going to Alif Shop for the SKU is no longer necessary.

figures.caption: Searching for an existing product while adding an offer.

steps.subhead: Price next to other sellers’ offers
paragraphs: Partners told us they look at competitors when setting a price. We added the prices of similar products right inside the offer form. That way the comparison happens at the moment you set your own price.

figures.caption: Other sellers’ prices in the offer form.

sections.title: From a request to handing over the goods

paragraphs: Handling an order takes a different path: spot a new request, open it and arrange the handover. Partners used to hear about new requests from the call centre. The workspace carries notifications for that.

figures.caption: Notifications about requests, delivery and stock.

paragraphs: The paperwork that used to go through terminals moved into the panel I designed. Delivery and self-pickup were separated, keeping the business logic intact. The handover method determines what the employee does next.

figures.caption: Orders in the delivery section.

paragraphs: A chat with the bank was added to the workspace. A partner can ask for help while working with products and orders.

figures.caption: A chat with the bank inside the workspace.

paragraphs: I designed the mobile version separately: notifications, products and delivery can be handled in the store, in the warehouse and at the pickup point.

figures.caption: Handling notifications, products and delivery from a phone.

paragraphs: The web and mobile versions of the workspace were designed. The main decisions are collected below.

cards.label: Partner autonomy
cards.title: An order without the bank stepping in
cards.text: The partner runs the order without the bank being involved at every step.
cards.measure: the share of orders handled by the partner alone

cards.label: Process quality
cards.title: Products, prices and terms in one flow
cards.text: Products, prices and terms are checked in a single flow.
cards.measure: the share of requests completed without cancellation

cards.label: Processing speed
cards.title: Order and delivery in one process
cards.text: The order and the delivery are linked in one working process.
cards.measure: the median time from request to handover for delivery

cards.label: Scalability
cards.title: A moderator only where control is needed
cards.text: Moderators step in only where a situation needs oversight.
cards.measure: the number of active partners per moderator

context.title: From a landing page to a dashboard
context.text: EAJ Trader already had an identity, a landing page and a list of future features. The next step was a dashboard for opening accounts, managing funds and keeping track of operations.

task.title: Define the first version
task.text: I was responsible for the structure of the dashboard and the logic of its main actions. Together with the client I chose which features would go into the MVP and how to connect the overview of funds, the accounts and the financial operations.

paragraphs: The client handed over preliminary research and a list of features. I compared the scenarios of different user types, from a beginner to an active trader. For the MVP we settled on the active trader.

blocks.text: The main path through the dashboard

steps.title: Assess the funds
steps.text: Look at the balance and the available amounts.

steps.title: Choose an account
steps.text: Find the right account and check its status.

steps.title: Go to an operation
steps.text: Choose a deposit, a withdrawal or a transfer.

paragraphs: The table maps the user types to their tasks. This is analysis material from the start of the project.

figures.caption: A comparison of the scenarios of different trader types. Research material from the project.

paragraphs: On the main screen I brought together the total balance, the information about funds and the entry points to the core operations. From here you can open an account, go to your accounts, top up the balance or withdraw funds. That way the overview of capital connects directly to what happens next.

figures.caption: An overview of funds and the entry points to the core operations.

paragraphs: I prepared two options for the trading accounts. A table is compact when there are many accounts. A card gathers the balance, the status and the actions around a single account.
The concepts were tested with 5 participants. Cards went into the MVP, and the table was kept as an option for working with a large number of accounts.

figures.caption: Concept 2. Accounts shown as cards.
figures.label: Concept 2 · Card view

figures.caption: Concept 1. Accounts shown as a table.
figures.label: Concept 1 · Table view

paragraphs: The client and I brought these operations together in the Funding section. Inside it the user chooses what to do with their funds. The entry points to deposits and withdrawals stayed on the main screen.

figures.caption: Deposits, withdrawals and internal transfers in one section.

paragraphs: For questions about the dashboard I designed Claims & Complaints. The user sees the list of support requests and their statuses, opens the conversation, adds details and attaches documents. The conversation can be picked up again from the same section.

figures.caption: Support requests and their current statuses.
The conversation for the selected support request.

paragraphs: The dashboard launched with an overview of funds and accounts. The financial operations and support were designed as well.

cards.label: Activation
cards.title: The path to a first deposit
cards.text: We put together the path from signing in to opening and funding a trading account.
cards.measure: conversion to opening and funding an account

cards.label: Account management
cards.title: A format for frequent operations
cards.text: For the MVP we chose the format that suits frequent operations on trading accounts.
cards.measure: the median time to complete the key account scenario

cards.label: Financial operations
cards.title: Clear operation statuses
cards.text: We made the statuses of deposits, withdrawals and transfers visible and clear.
cards.measure: the share of funded accounts with a repeat operation

cards.label: In-product support
cards.title: Support requests inside the dashboard
cards.text: A support request is created and tracked inside the dashboard, with no need to look for an external contact.
cards.measure: the share of successfully completed deposits, withdrawals and transfers

cases.title: Namaste
cases.subtitle: How we chose the features of a workout app’s first version

meta.Команда: Product Designer, Product Owner, Developer, Product Manager

context.title: More ideas than resources
context.text: The team wanted to combine workouts, habit building and health features. The list had different practices, difficulty levels, personalization, sleep, water, nutrition and activity. For the first version we had to pick what mattered most.

task.title: Build the core of the app
task.text: I designed the path to a suitable class and took part in choosing the extra features for the MVP.

sections.title: First I worked out how to help someone start practising

paragraphs: Before designing any screens I had to understand how to help a person choose a direction that suits them and reach their first workout without a complicated setup. I studied yoga and mindfulness apps and compared onboarding, personalization, class structure and subscription models.

figures.caption: The original analysis of workout apps. Research material from the project.

after: The research showed two approaches. In some apps a person started a workout quickly but could barely tailor the experience. In others the personalization went deeper, but the start was overloaded with questions. For Namaste I chose something in between: a short survey establishes the direction, the level and the class format, and then the user moves on to a programme that fits.

paragraphs: I built the app’s structure around a single cycle: a person chooses a direction, takes a class and comes back for the next workout. The health features support the core scenario without competing with the workouts on the main screen.

figures.caption: The app’s structure and its main sections.

sections.title: How a user picks a class

paragraphs: On first launch the user sets a direction and a level. Then they move to the classes and open the description of a suitable workout. The app has three difficulty levels: beginner, advanced and master.

sections.title: From the list to the workout

paragraphs: After choosing the parameters the user moves to the classes and opens a workout description. These screens show the main screen, the list of exercises and a class card.

sections.title: What to do about the health features

paragraphs: After the core scenario we came back to the extra features. We compared their value, the development effort and the monetization options. Sleep and water went into the first version. The calorie counter was postponed, and the pedometer and activity tracking needed their integrations checked.

items.label: Test
items.title: 6 respondents
items.text: The health features were tested using Feature Testing.

items.label: Observation
items.title: Sleep and water fit alongside the workouts
items.text: Participants saw these features as a fitting part of the app.

items.label: Evaluation
items.title: Practice consistency
items.text: Individual workouts form a consistent practice. Impact was evaluated using: return frequency and D7 and D30 retention after the first workout.

paragraphs: We launched an iOS app with a training cycle, three difficulty levels and the sleep and water health features.

cards.label: Personalized start
cards.title: A short onboarding
cards.text: We made a short onboarding that helps people choose a direction, a level and a class format that suits them.
cards.measure: the share of users who complete their first workout

cards.label: Practice consistency
cards.title: A continuous training cycle
cards.text: We joined the separate classes into one continuous training cycle.
cards.measure: D7 and D30 retention after the first workout

cards.label: MVP scope
cards.title: Sleep and water health features
cards.text: We selected the health features by user value and implementation effort.
cards.measure: health feature usage among active users

cards.label: Monetization
cards.title: A free experience before the subscription
cards.text: We kept a free experience that shows the product’s value before anyone subscribes.
cards.measure: conversion to a subscription and the renewal rate

cases.title: 360 Tracker
cases.subtitle: A family map, geofences and different privacy rules

meta.Команда: Product Designer, Product Owner, Developer, Product Manager

context.title: A family tracker from scratch
context.text: 360 Tracker helps you find out where the people close to you are and get in touch with them. The map, the family circle and notifications about leaving a geofence had to come together in one app.

task.title: Account for the whole family’s needs
task.text: I designed the core scenarios and the geolocation settings. I had to define the MVP knowing that parents, children and adult members have different expectations about access to a location.

paragraphs: First we discussed the product’s goals with the stakeholders. Then I compared Kids360, Kid Security, iSharing and Family Tracker: how each handles the map, geofences, notifications, trip history and the subscription.
The first version included the map, the family circle, statuses, geofences and the connection between members. Complex analytics and extended settings were postponed.

blocks.text: What went into the first version

steps.title: The map and the family circle
steps.text: Members, their location and the time of the last update.

steps.title: Contact between members
steps.text: A group chat and private conversations.

paragraphs: The map, geofences, notifications, trip history and the approaches to a subscription. Below is the analysis material from the project.

figures.caption: A comparison of family tracker features. Material from the project.
A comparison of subscription models. Material from the project.

paragraphs: I built the app’s structure around the family circle. Once people have been added, the user sees them on the map, gets notifications about the events that matter and can turn to the trip history when needed.

figures.caption: The main sections of the family tracker.

paragraphs: The map became the main screen. On it you can select a family member, see their location and the time of the last update. Geofences cover the places that matter.

figures.caption: The map, the list of members and the places that matter.

sections.title: From an event to an action

paragraphs: If a child leaves the boundary of a zone, the app shows a notification. From it you can go to the location or to a message.

figures.caption: A notification about leaving a zone, and the location on the map.
figures.alt: A notification with the actions Message and Location next to the map

paragraphs: The family circle has a group chat and private conversations: you can check what happened, ask for a location, send a photo or a file.

figures.caption: The group chat, private conversations and the family circle.

sections.title: Hiding a location needed more work

items.label: The idea
items.title: Controlling your own visibility
items.text: We proposed letting people hide their location temporarily and choose zones where they do not appear. We assumed adults would want to control their own visibility.

items.label: Test
items.title: A question in the child’s scenario
items.text: In testing, the capability itself was received well. But a question came up in the parent’s scenario: what happens if a child hides their location and the parent loses access to it?

items.label: Decision
items.title: Different rules for adults and children
items.text: After the test we changed the rules. Adults control their own visibility, while for a child profile a parent can restrict hiding. One setting ended up with different rules for different family members.

blocks.subhead: Different rules for adults and children
paragraphs: An adult controls their own visibility. On a child profile, the option to hide a location is controlled by a parent. One setting ended up with different rules for different family members.

figures.caption: Controlling the visibility of a location.

paragraphs: 30 days of route history went into the MVP as a paid feature. It is available to the owner of the data and is not opened to the rest of the circle automatically. The basic scenarios stayed free.

figures.caption: Route history and the choice of period.

paragraphs: We launched an iOS app with the map, geofences and notifications.

cards.label: Family activation
cards.title: The family circle comes first
cards.text: We made creating the family circle and adding people the first key scenario.
cards.measure: the share of users who create a circle and add a member

cards.label: Map and statuses
cards.title: Location and status on one screen
cards.text: We brought the location and the current state of each member onto one screen.
cards.measure: D7 and D30 retention among activated families

cards.label: Geofences and notifications
cards.title: Notifications instead of watching the map
cards.text: We added notifications about the events that matter, so nobody has to keep watching the map.
cards.measure: the share of active users who use geofences and notifications

cards.label: Freemium
cards.title: Safety free, history by subscription
cards.text: We kept the basic safety features free and put trip history into the extended plan.
cards.measure: conversion of active families to a subscription and the renewal rate
